title: The entrance
hookLine: the procession, the sign of the cross, and the priest kissing the altar

cards: Sunday morning. People drift in: families wrestling toddlers, an old man with a cane, teenagers who got dragged. Some kneel and pray.
Some chat in whispers. Some scroll their phones until the last second. Then a bell rings, or the organ starts, and everyone stands.
A guest at Mass can feel a step behind: everyone else seems to know when to stand, what to say, where to look.
So for the next two weeks, i'll walk you through the Catholic Mass one scene at a time, the way you'd walk someone through a play they've never seen.

teach.b: First, a procession comes up the aisle while everyone sings. At the front, someone carries a cross on a tall pole, with candles on either side. Sometimes incense, swinging in a metal holder.
Then the servers, a reader, and a deacon holding up a large book of the Gospels.
The priest walks last. Everyone is walking toward the same thing: the altar. When the priest reaches it, he bows, and then he does something a first-time visitor may not expect.
He leans down and kisses it. Why kiss a table? Catholics see the altar as a sign of Christ himself, and it's where the sacrifice of the Mass will be offered.

There's an old reason too. Tradition says early Christians gathered for Mass at the tombs of martyrs, and today some altars hold a small relic of a saint. That cloud of witnesses from last week is built into the altar.

teach.h: THE SIGN OF THE CROSS, TOGETHER.
teach.b: Then the priest turns to the people, and the whole church makes the sign of the cross together, the one you learned on your very first day. Then he greets them.
In Latin, Dominus vobiscum: the Lord be with you. In the book of Ruth, a farmer named Boaz walks into his field and says to the workers, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord be with you." They answer back.
And that's the point of the entrance. Before anyone prays, before anyone reads, before the bread, the people come together. The Mass isn't something you watch.
It's something a gathered crowd does.

how: At the start of Mass the congregation stands and sings as the priest and ministers process to the altar; the priest kisses the altar, everyone makes the sign of the cross together, and the priest greets the people, who answer him.

games.q: who does what at the entrance — tap the pairs.
p: carries the book of the Gospels
walks last, then kisses the altar
greeted his workers: the Lord be with you

s: the priest kisses the altar because it's a sign of Christ
Catholics see the altar as a sign of Christ, where the sacrifice of the Mass is offered.
altars never have anything inside them
some hold a small relic of a saint, a custom tradition traces to Masses at martyrs' tombs.
the greeting the Lord be with you was invented for the Mass
it's old. in the book of Ruth, Boaz says it to the workers in his field.

games.q: you're the priest. the procession has reached the front, and you're standing at the altar. what do you do first?
o: open the book and start reading.
games.why: he bows and kisses the altar. only then does he turn, make the sign of the cross with everyone, and greet them.

practice: Think of the next place you're going, work, a class, a dinner, and picture getting there five minutes early: not to answer emails in the parking lot, just to arrive, and notice the room, the people coming in, the light.
If you pray, ask God to be with the people you'll meet there. If you don't, just be the one who got there first, and let it settle.

wordCard.voice: The entrance. The Mass begins with a procession, a kissed altar, the sign of the cross and a greeting.

orig.note: Latin: the Lord be with you, the priest's greeting. the people answer, et cum spiritu tuo: and with your spirit.

carryVoice: Your line: we gather first. A kiss for the altar, a greeting for the people. Day one hundred and four.
